title: A principal components model of soundscape perception
research_question: To identify underlying dimensions of soundscape perception, to develop an empirically grounded model integrating perceptual attributes into basic dimensions, and to determine relationships among these basic perceptual dimensions and physical soundscape properties, including categories of dominant sounds and acoustic variables.

participants.description: 48 women, 52 men; mean age 25.6 years, range 19–54 years. University students in Stockholm, Sweden. All had absolute hearing thresholds below 25 dB in their best ear at tested frequencies (0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8 kHz).
participants.recruitment: Participants received a small monetary compensation.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 50 binaural recordings of urban outdoor soundscapes, 30 seconds in duration, from London and Stockholm. Selected to cover a wide range of sound-pressure levels (43–79 dB LAeq,30s) and diversity of environmental sounds (technology, humans, nature). Each excerpt included ambiance and more than one single sound event, representative of its location.

measures.instrument: 116 unidirectional attribute scales (e.g., 'pleasant', 'calm') on a 100-mm visual analog scale ('attribute-soundscape match').
Dichotomous variables (Technological, Human, Natural Sounds) based on independent listening assessments by three research team members.
A-weighted equivalent continuous sound-pressure level (LAeq,30s) and Zwicker loudness (N10).
Difference between levels exceeded 10 and 90% of the time (LA10-LA90) and Zwicker loudness (N10-N90).
Difference between A- and C-weighted sound-pressure level (LCeq,30s-LAeq,30s, or Lc-A).

findings.quote: Component 1, 2 and 3 explained 50, 18, and 6%, respectively, of the variance in the data set.

mechanisms: Principal Components Analysis (PCA) identifies underlying dimensions of soundscape perception by integrating a large set of perceptual attributes into a smaller number of basic components.

The relationships between these basic perceptual dimensions and physical soundscape properties (acoustic measures and dominant sound categories) are meaningful, supporting the interpretation of the components.
Informational properties (sound categories) contribute substantially to soundscape perception over and above overall loudness, suggesting that the type of sound matters beyond its intensity.

The circumplex model of affect (Russell) provides a framework for understanding how Pleasantness and Eventfulness combine to form different soundscape experiences (e.g., exciting, calm, chaotic, monotonous).
moderators: Overall soundscape loudness (N10) was found to moderate the relationship between dominant sound categories and Pleasantness/Eventfulness.
implementation_implications: The proposed principal components model provides a framework for future soundscape research and practice, suggesting which basic dimensions (Pleasantness, Eventfulness, Familiarity) are necessary to measure.
The model suggests how to measure these dimensions using a defined set of attribute scales.
The model provides guidance on how to promote high-quality soundscapes through abatement and promotion of specific sound categories.
To obtain an activating, exciting, and fascinating soundscape, promotion of human sounds (e.g., from playgrounds and cafeterias) is suggested.
To make a pleasant soundscape calmer, abatement of human sounds is suggested.
Adding or promoting natural sounds may not improve soundscape quality in situations with detectable adverse sounds (e.g., distant road-traffic noise) due to masking issues.

limitations: The variance in Familiarity was rather low, suggesting that urban soundscapes in general are perceived as similar in terms of familiarity for listeners from the same cultural setting, limiting its importance for applied work.

The relationships between sound-categories and basic components of soundscape perception are not absolute truths; unpleasant natural sounds and pleasant technological sounds might exist, though not common in modern urban outdoor environments.

The study acknowledges that adding or promoting natural sounds may be difficult to accomplish in situations with detectable adverse sounds, such as distant road-traffic noise, because positive natural sounds would not easily mask low-frequency components of such noises.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: There is a need for a model that identifies underlying dimensions of soundscape perception, and which may guide measurement and improvement of soundscape quality. With the purpose to develop such a model, a listening experiment was conducted. One hundred listeners measured 50 excerpts of binaural recordings of urban outdoor soundscapes on 116 attribute scales. The average attribute scale values were subjected to principal components analysis, resulting in three components: Pleasantness, eventfulness, and familiarity, explaining 50, 18 and 6% of the total variance, respectively. The principal-component scores were correlated with physical soundscape properties, including categories of dominant sounds and acoustic variables. Soundscape excerpts dominated by technological sounds were found to be unpleasant, whereas soundscape excerpts dominated by natural sounds were pleasant, and soundscape excerpts dominated by human sounds were eventful. These relationships remained after controlling for the overall soundscape loudness (Zwicker’s N10), which shows that ‘informational’ properties are substantial contributors to the perception of soundscape. The proposed principal components model provides a framework for future soundscape research and practice. In particular, it suggests which basic dimensions are necessary to measure, how to measure them by a defined set of attribute scales, and how to promote high-quality soundscapes.
